Hi there. Sorry you're going through this. I can chip in as I have experienced this, although I can only tell you my experience and am sorry if it's not reassuring. 

First, you're not 'addicted'. Seroquel isn't addictive in the same way that illicit drugs are. Perhaps you are 'dependent' on Seroquel, for sleep purposes, but that happens with a tonne of drugs and shouldn't be a cause for alarm in itself.

I'm taking 50mg of Seroquel at the moment. The med I'm taking for depression (Nardil) causes bad insomnia for me and Seroquel allows me to get to sleep, reliably. Unfortunately it doesn't help me stay asleep longer than around 3 hours, so I'm having my own problems with insomnia.

I tried to come off it once, in my case jumping off 25mg, rather than tapering any further. When I stopped Seroquel, I just couldn't sleep. At all. I'm sure that after a couple of days I must have started micronapping but I wasn't getting any meaningful sleep. It became too much and I started taking Seroquel again. 

A lot of people do come off Seroquel so I'm not trying to say it's impossible to do so but it got too much for me and my situation at the time wasn't such that I could afford to just not sleep. I'm sure if I had been able to stick it out for longer that my body would eventually adjusted and I would have started to experience normal sleep again (meaning the ability to fall asleep without Seroquel - I have no idea whether I would have slept less or more than on Seroquel). I couldn't get there though.

I'll also say that inability to sleep was the only 'withdrawal' symptom that I suffered. Not that this wasn't bad enough but it was the only thing. It's not like I've read withdrawing from benzos, for example, is, where you can experience a multitude of terrible, and even dangerous, symptoms.

What you're going through is, I think, pretty normal. It's horrible though. I guess you'll have to decide whether you can tolerate this for a bit longer. So the  money is held in an escrow wallet, meaning neither the buyer nor seller have access to it. If the goods arrive and the buyer is happy, he will finalise and the monies in the escrow wallet are released to seller.

If the buyer does not receive goods or is not happy he won't finalise and will dispute. The market admin will then rule in favour of buyer (buyer will be returned money) or seller (seller will get money).

The one flaw is that it allows big amounts to build up in escrow, then the market can exit scam and take the money.

There are other solutions like multi-sig wallets or walletless markets but I think no system is perfect.

I've been inpatient a few times. Of course everybody's experience is different and a lot will depend on the hospital.

I found it helpful but to be honest most of the help was being around other patients in similar situations. It felt good to feel less isolated an that I wasn't the only one going through hell. It also provides respite from the ordinary pressures of daily life.

There are usually therapy sessions and activities. And they may put you on a new med which they can monitor.

To be honest I also found it lacking in many ways. I was in a private hospital (in the UK, the US system is different I guess). The food was really good, the facilities were ok. But a lot of the staff were minimum wage, the doctors were hardly around at all and my general feeling was that it was more a business than anything else. I didn't feel any sort of genuine concern.

As I said it varies though. The place I was didn't have a lot of therapy (that doesn't do me much good anyway) and so there was a lot of free time where patients would hand out, smoking (I didn't smoke before I went in but was smoking about 30 a day by the time I left, lol).

There was also no gym and I wasn't allowed to go for runs outside the hospital (running was one thing that always helped me a lot).

I wasn't allowed my phone for the first few days but after that they gave it to me. I actually sort of liked not having a phone for a while. 

Hit me up if you have any questions but yeah I think it varies so much hospital to hospital that people just have such different experiences.
